program_plain: World: a 64x64 lattice of cells (wrap-around edges) with 400 scattered items of 2 kinds and 20 mobile walkers. Rules each step: each walker steps to a random neighbouring cell; an unladen walker picks up an item with probability (0.1/(0.1+f))^2, and a laden walker drops its item with probability (f/(0.3+f))^2, where f is the fraction of items of the same kind it met in its last 10 steps.
model_family: Swarm intelligence / stigmergy: agent-based lattice (cellular-automaton-like) ant clustering and brood-sorting model
standard_name: Deneubourg et al. ant-inspired clustering and sorting model (brood sorting / cemetery organization); Lumer-Faieta ant clustering

full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Deneubourg et al. (1991) ant-inspired clustering and sorting model. I did not read the full text of the 1991 paper. My match to it rests on the rule form and on secondary descriptions in the search results.

**1. Model family.** This is swarm intelligence and stigmergy, in the form of a cellular-automaton or lattice agent model. Random-walking agents pick up and drop items with probabilities that depend on a local item density. That density is estimated from a short memory of recent encounters, here the last 10 steps. It is the "brood sorting" or "cemetery organisation" model.

**2. The specific behaviour.** One item kind gives clustering, and two kinds give sorting into separate piles. The scattered items coarsen over time into a few large clusters, and in the long run into a single cluster. This matches your observations: Moran's I is high and rising, and one domain dominates. Your "many separate domains" reading (g_n_domains = −2.0) is probably a sign convention for few domains. I am assuming that, and I have not checked it.

**3. Sources I checked against search results.**
- **Earliest source.** Deneubourg, Goss, Franks, Sendova-Franks, Detrain and Chrétien, "The dynamics of collective sorting: robot-like ants and ant-like robots", in *From Animals to Animats* (Proc. 1st Int. Conf. on Simulation of Adaptive Behavior, MIT Press, 1991, pp. 356–363).
  - A later paper summarises it as a simulation showing that simple agents could achieve two generic tasks: clustering scattered objects of one type, and grouping and sorting objects of two types.
  - It adds that for sorting, the agents needed to sense local densities of the different types, with short-term memory, and to know the type of item they were carrying. That is the structure of your rule, with its fraction f over the last 10 steps.
  - Clustering was the result of the mechanism operating on a single type of item. This corresponds to your "1 kind of item" variant.
  - The squared-threshold form, (k/(k+f))², is the one I remember from that paper. I did not see the formula in the snippets, so that part comes from memory.
- **Physics treatment.** Bonabeau, Theraulaz, Fourcassié and Deneubourg, "Phase-ordering kinetics of cemetery organization in ants", *Physical Review E* 57(4), 1998, pp. 4568–4571. The search returned only reference-list entries for it, so I confirmed the citation but not its content. It frames the coarsening as phase-ordering kinetics, which fits your rising Moran's I and shrinking domain count.
- **Extension to data.** Lumer and Faieta, "Diversity and adaptation in populations of clustering ants", *Proc. 3rd Int. Conf. on Simulation of Adaptive Behavior (From Animals to Animats 3)*, MIT Press, 1994, pp. 501–508. Reference lists confirm the title, venue and year. A later summary says Lumer and Faieta introduced further developments and extended its application to clustering data objects.
- **Review.** Bonabeau, Dorigo and Theraulaz, *Swarm Intelligence: From Natural to Artificial Systems*, Oxford University Press, 1999. A Scholarpedia entry describes the same model: an unloaded ant picks up with probability inversely related to local density, and a loaded ant drops with probability that rises with local density of similar items. It also notes the model has been validated against experimental data from real ants.
- **Cellular-automaton version.** A cellular-automaton variant reports that probabilistic pick-up yields compact clusters and speeds up clustering, and in the long run a single cluster emerges. It also reports that with several corpse species, the algorithm sorts them into distinct clusters.

**4. Variants and caveats.**
- The 40-walker variant should give faster coarsening, and I expect it to differ only in rate.
- With two item kinds, the literature mainly reports sorting into segregated clusters. Your "one cell-type fills most of the lattice" feature likely reflects domain coarsening in the final state. I did not check that.
- With 400 items on 4096 cells, coarsening may be slow and incomplete. That is a finite-time effect, not a new phenomenon.
- I found no source describing exactly your parameters (64×64, 400 items, 20 walkers, thresholds 0.1 and 0.3, memory of 10). Parameter values do not change the qualitative behaviour.

**5. Confidence: high.** The rule structure matches the Deneubourg model, and several independent sources describe the same phenomenon. The main gap is that I could not read the primary papers directly.
